mainTopic: Healthy and harmful foods, hilly cities and aging, squaring a city to the true directions for תחום שבת, and שמואל's rules about the timing of the תקופות.
overview: This amud opens at the end of a קשיא. A ברייתא calls ירק (vegetables) harmful, which seems to clash with רב הונא's praise of vegetables. The גמרא answers that רב הונא means garlic and leeks. A ברייתא calls צנון (radish) an elixir of life, and another calls it deadly; the גמרא settles this by plant part (leaves vs. roots) or by season (summer vs. winter). Next, רב יהודה quotes רב that hilly cities make people 'die at half their days.' The גמרא corrects this to 'age at half their days,' and רב הונא בריה דרב יהושע confirms it from his own life. The גמרא then returns to תחום שבת: a city's square must line up with the true compass directions, found by the stars. רבי יוסי offers a backup method using the sun's seasonal path, supported by a פסוק in קהלת, but רב משרשיא rejects the solstice part of that method. Finally, שמואל teaches the fixed times when each of the four תקופות begins, the 91-day-and-7.5-hour math behind them, and the harm that comes when a season begins in the hour of צדק.

steps.title: The list of harmful things ends with vegetables
steps.stepSummary: The tail end of a ברייתא listing harmful foods, which includes ירק (vegetables).
steps.whatsHappening: We are joining the גמרא in the middle of a challenge. A ברייתא lists three harmful things, and the last one is vegetables.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Just before this, רב הונא said a תלמיד חכם should not live in a city without vegetables, which implies vegetables are good. This ברייתא says vegetables are harmful. That contradiction is the קשיא the גמרא must now solve.

keyTerms.meaning: Coarse bread made from flour that was not finely sifted

steps.confusionAlert: This amud starts in the middle of a quote. The words 'coarse bread, new beer, and vegetables' are the end of a list of harmful foods. They are not a new statement.

phrases.english: Coarse bread
phrases.notes: Item one in the ברייתא's list of harmful things

phrases.english: and new beer, and vegetables.
phrases.notes: Vegetables are listed as harmful, which causes the contradiction

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes a challenge that began on the previous amud.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב הונא's statement that a תלמיד חכם should live only where vegetables are available.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If vegetables are harmful, why would a scholar need to live where they are available?

steps.title: Garlic and leeks versus other vegetables
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the two sources are talking about different kinds of vegetables.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is not difficult. This one refers to garlic and leeks; that one refers to other vegetables.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא solves the contradiction by splitting the vegetables into two groups.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב הונא's praise of vegetables refers to garlic and leeks, which are healthy. The ברייתא that calls vegetables harmful refers to other vegetables. Each source is right about its own group.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not difficult. This phrase introduces an answer.

phrases.english: It is not difficult:
this one refers to garlic and leeks,
that one refers to other vegetables.
phrases.notes: 'That one' is the ברייתא that calls vegetables harmful.

steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases: each source refers to a different type of vegetable.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both sources seemed to be talking about all vegetables.
steps.terutzMaskana: Garlic and leeks are healthy; other vegetables are harmful.

steps.title: A ברייתא praises garlic, leeks, and radish
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא supports the answer by calling garlic a real vegetable, leeks half a vegetable, and radish an 'elixir of life.'
steps.simpleTranslation: As it was taught: Garlic is a vegetable. Leeks are half a vegetable. If you have seen a radish, you have seen an elixir of life.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to support its answer that some vegetables are healthy.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Garlic is called fully 'vegetable' in the good, healthy sense. Leeks are half as healthy. Radish is praised very highly. This shows that חז"ל did not see all vegetables as harmful.

keyTerms.meaning: As it was taught in a ברייתא
Elixir of life; a life-giving medicine

phrases.english: As it was taught: Garlic is a (healthy) vegetable;
leeks are half a vegetable;
phrases.notes: Meaning they're only half as healthy.

phrases.english: if radish has been seen, an elixir of life has been seen.

steps.raayaObject: The claim that garlic and leeks are healthy vegetables.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא ranking garlic, leeks, and radish as beneficial.

steps.title: Another ברייתא calls radish deadly
steps.stepSummary: A different ברייתא says seeing a radish is like seeing a deadly poison, which contradicts the ברייתא just quoted.
steps.simpleTranslation: But wasn't it taught: If radish has been seen, a deadly drug has been seen!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the ברייתא from step 3 with a second ברייתא that says the exact opposite about radish.
steps.deeperAnalysis: One ברייתא calls radish an 'elixir of life.' Another calls it a 'drug of death.' Both cannot be true in the same situation, so the גמרא needs to explain the difference.

keyTerms.meaning: But wasn't it taught? This phrase introduces a contradicting source.

phrases.english: But wasn't it taught: if radish has been seen,
a deadly drug has been seen!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָא תַנְיָא: נִרְאֶה צְנוֹן — נִרְאֶה סַם הַמָּוֶת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the ברייתא used as proof in step 3.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא calling radish an 'elixir of life.'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Two ברייתות say opposite things about radish.

steps.title: Radish leaves versus radish roots
steps.stepSummary: First answer: one ברייתא speaks about the leaves and the other about the root.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is not difficult. Here it refers to the leaves; there it refers to the roots.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא resolves the contradiction by saying each ברייתא talks about a different part of the radish.
steps.deeperAnalysis: One explanation is that the ברייתא that calls radish deadly refers to the leaves. The ברייתא that praises it refers to the root. So the radish has a healthy part and a harmful part.

keyTerms.meaning: Literally 'mothers'; here, the roots (the main body of the radish)

phrases.english: It is not difficult: here it refers to the leaves,
phrases.notes: 'Here' is the ברייתא that calls radish deadly.

phrases.english: there it refers to the roots.
phrases.notes: 'There' is the ברייתא that praises radish.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא קַשְׁיָא: כָּאן — בֶּעָלִין, כָּאן — בָּאִמָּהוֹת
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases by the part of the plant.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both ברייתות seemed to describe the whole radish.
steps.terutzMaskana: The leaves are harmful; the root is beneficial.

steps.title: Radish in summer versus winter
steps.stepSummary: Second answer: one ברייתא speaks about the summer and the other about the rainy season.
steps.simpleTranslation: Here it refers to the summer; there it refers to the rainy season.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers a different way to settle the same contradiction, this time based on the season.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Instead of splitting by plant part, this answer splits by season. Radish is healthy in summer and harmful in the rainy winter months. Each ברייתא describes a different time of year.
steps.whatToRemember: Radish is praised in one ברייתא and condemned in another. The גמרא explains this either by plant part (leaves vs. roots) or by season (summer vs. winter).

phrases.english: Here it refers to the summer,
phrases.notes: This is when radish is good for you.

phrases.english: there it refers to the rainy season.
phrases.notes: This is when radish is harmful.

steps.triggerLanguage: כָּאן — בִּימוֹת הַחַמָּה, כָּאן — בִּימוֹת הַגְּשָׁמִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second, independent answer to the same קשיא from step 4.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Radish has the same effect all year round.
steps.terutzMaskana: Radish is beneficial in summer and harmful in winter.

steps.title: Hilly cities shorten life
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה quotes רב: in a city full of steep ups and downs, people and animals die at half their days.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said that רב said: Any city that has ascents and descents, the people and animals in it die at half their days.
steps.whatsHappening: A new teaching about how a city's geography affects health, continuing the theme of what makes a place healthy.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב says that constantly climbing up and down hills wears down the body. As stated, it claims that people in such towns die at half their normal lifespan. The גמרא will question this wording next.

keyTerms.meaning: At half their days; at half their expected lifespan

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said that Rav said:

phrases.aramaic: כׇּל עִיר שֶׁיֵּשׁ בָּהּ מַעֲלוֹת וּמוֹרָדוֹת,
phrases.english: any city that has ascents and descents,
the people and animals in it
die at half their days.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר רַב: כׇּל עִיר שֶׁיֵּשׁ בָּהּ מַעֲלוֹת וּמוֹרָדוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new statement on the related theme of healthy and unhealthy places.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Hilly terrain is physically draining and harms the lifespan of the city's people and animals.

steps.title: Do they really die young?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא questions the wording: could רב really mean they actually die early?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the literal meaning of רב's statement.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Everyone could see that people in hilly towns live normal lifespans. So the literal word 'die' cannot be what רב meant. This sets up a correction of the wording.

keyTerms.meaning: Would it enter your mind? A way of rejecting a reading as impossible.

steps.confusionAlert: The question looks like a simple question, but it is really an attack. The גמרא is saying that reading 'die' literally makes no sense.

phrases.english: 'Die' — can that enter your mind?

steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Reality shows that people in hilly cities do not actually die at half their lifespan.

steps.title: They age early, not die early
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא corrects the wording: they grow old at half their days.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, say: they grow old at half their days.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא fixes the wording of רב's statement to answer the challenge.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The constant strain of the hills makes people look and feel old early. It does not shorten their lives. The word 'die' is replaced with 'grow old.'

keyTerms.meaning: Rather, say. This phrase introduces a corrected reading.

phrases.english: Rather, say:
they grow old at half their days.

steps.terutzResolutionType: Correcting the wording of the statement.

steps.title: The hills aged רב הונא בריה דרב יהושע
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא בריה דרב יהושע says the hills between בי בירי and בי נרש made him old.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא בריה דרב יהושע said: These ascents of בי בירי and בי נרש made me old.
steps.whatsHappening: An אמורא supports the corrected reading from his own experience.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב הונא בריה דרב יהושע lived in a hilly area. He says the climbing there made him age early. This confirms the corrected reading 'they grow old.'
steps.whatToRemember: רב's statement means that hilly cities cause early aging, not early death. רב הונא בריה דרב יהושע testifies to this from his own life.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב הוּנָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב יְהוֹשֻׁעַ:
phrases.english: Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua, said:
these ascents of Bei Biri
and of Bei Neresh made me old.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב הוּנָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב יְהוֹשֻׁעַ: הָנֵי מוּלְיָיתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the corrected reading from step 9.
steps.raayaObject: The claim that hilly terrain causes premature aging.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The personal testimony of רב הונא בריה דרב יהושע.

steps.title: Squaring a city along the compass directions
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that when squaring a city to measure the תחום, the square must line up with true north and south.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: If one comes to square a city, he squares it according to the square of the world. He sets its northern side to the north of the world and its southern side to the south of the world.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא leaves the health topic and returns to the main subject of the פרק: measuring תחום שבת around a city.
steps.deeperAnalysis: To measure the תחום, an imaginary square is drawn around the city, and the 2000 אמה are measured from there. This ברייתא adds that the square must face the real compass directions. It may not be tilted to match the city's own irregular shape.

keyTerms.meaning: To square it (to enclose the city in a square)
The square of the world; the four compass directions

steps.confusionAlert: 'Squaring' does not mean following the city's own shape. It means drawing a square whose sides face true north, south, east, and west.
steps.whyThisMatters: This rule fixes the exact shape of the city's boundary for תחום שבת. It decides where the 2000 אמה begin and how far a person may walk on שבת.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught: If one comes to square it (the city),
he squares it according to the square of the world;
he sets its northern side to the north of the world
and its southern side to the south of the world.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns from the health tangent to the laws of measuring a city's תחום.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The square drawn around a city for תחום purposes must be aligned with the true compass directions.

steps.title: The stars as a sign for north and south
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא gives a sign for finding the directions: the Great Bear is in the north and Scorpio is in the south.
steps.simpleTranslation: And your sign: the Wagon (Ursa Major) is in the north, and the Scorpion is in the south.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא finishes its rule with a practical tip for finding north and south.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule requires lining the square up with true north and south, so a person needs a reliable way to find them. The constellation עגלה (the Great Bear) appears in the northern sky, and עקרב (Scorpio) appears in the southern sky.

keyTerms.meaning: And your sign; a way to remember or identify something

steps.whatToRemember: A city's תחום square follows the true compass directions, and the stars (עגלה in the north, עקרב in the south) show where those directions are.

phrases.english: And your sign: the Wagon (Ursa Major) is in the north,
and the Scorpion is in the south.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the ברייתא from step 11 with a practical way to find the directions.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The northern and southern directions are found by the constellations עגלה and עקרב.

steps.title: רבי יוסי: Use the sun's seasonal path to find the directions
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוסי says that someone who cannot find the directions by the stars may use the seasons. The sun's path on the longest day marks north, its path on the shortest day marks south, and at the ניסן and תשרי equinoxes it rises due east and sets due west.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוסי says: If a person does not know how to square the city by the world's true directions, he may square it by the seasons. How? Where the sun rises and sets on the longest day, that is the north side. Where the sun rises and sets on the shortest day, that is the south side. At the spring equinox (תקופת ניסן) and the fall equinox (תקופת תשרי), the sun rises in the exact middle of the east and sets in the exact middle of the west.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוסי gives a backup method for finding north, south, east and west. It is for someone who cannot use the stars, as the previous ברייתא taught.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier ברייתא used the stars, which are precise. רבי יוסי adds a simpler method based on where the sun rises and sets in each season. In summer the sun's path leans north, in winter it leans south, and at the equinoxes it lines up exactly with east and west.

keyTerms.meaning: To square it, meaning to draw a square around the city for measuring the תחום
The 'square of the world', meaning the four true directions
A season. It also means the solstice or equinox that begins a season
The longest day of the year (summer solstice) and the shortest day (winter solstice)

steps.confusionAlert: רבי יוסי does not mean the sun rises in the north. On the longest day it rises toward the north side of the east and sets toward the north side of the west, so its whole path runs along the north.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yosei says:
If he does not know how to square it (the city)
by the square of the world (the true four directions),
he squares it according to the seasons.
phrases.notes: This is less exact than the stars, but easier.

phrases.english: How so?
Where the sun rises on the longest day
and sets on the longest day —
that is the north side.
Where the sun rises on the shortest day
and sets on the shortest day —
that is the south side.
At the spring equinox and the fall equinox —
the sun rises in the middle of the east
and sets in the middle of the west,

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יוֹסֵי אוֹמֵר: אִם אֵינוֹ יוֹדֵעַ לְרַבְּעָהּ בְּרִיבּוּעַ שֶׁל עוֹלָם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the ברייתא from steps 11-12 with רבי יוסי's backup method, for use when the star method is not available.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If you cannot use the stars, find the directions by the sun's path: summer path = north, winter path = south, equinox sunrise and sunset = due east and due west.

steps.title: A פסוק in קהלת supports the sun's path
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוסי supports his description with the פסוק in קהלת: the sun goes south by day and circles north at night. 'Round and round goes the רוח' refers to the east and west sides, which the sun sometimes crosses openly and sometimes circles around unseen.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it says: 'It goes toward the south and turns toward the north.' 'It goes toward the south' means by day, and 'turns toward the north' means at night. 'Round and round goes the רוח (direction)' refers to the east side and the west side. Sometimes the sun travels across them, and sometimes it goes around them.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוסי brings a פסוק from קהלת to back up his picture of how the sun moves.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק is read as describing the sun, not the wind. By day the sun travels across the southern part of the sky. At night it circles back around the north, out of sight. The word רוח is read as 'side' or 'direction', so the פסוק is talking about the east and west sides.

keyTerms.meaning: Goes toward the south, meaning the sun's path by day
Turns toward the north, meaning the sun's hidden path at night
Wind. Here it means a side or direction
Travels across them (seen) and circles around them (unseen)

steps.confusionAlert: Here הרוח does not mean the wind. It means 'the side' or 'the direction'.

phrases.english: As it is said: 'It goes toward the south'
'and turns toward the north,'
'It goes toward the south' — by day,
'and turns toward the north' — at night.
'Round and round goes the direction' —
these are the east side and the west side,
sometimes it (the sun) travels across them
and sometimes it circles around them.

steps.triggerLanguage: שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: ״הוֹלֵךְ אֶל דָּרוֹם וְסוֹבֵב אֶל צָפוֹן״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a פסוק as support for the sun's path that רבי יוסי described in step 13.
steps.raayaObject: רבי יוסי's description of the sun's path through the directions
steps.raayaSupportSource: קהלת 1:6, 'הולך אל דרום וסובב אל צפון, סובב סובב הולך הרוח'

steps.title: רב משרשיא rejects the solstice rules
steps.stepSummary: רב משרשיא says these rules are not reliable. A ברייתא teaches that the sun never rises in the far northeast corner and sets in the far northwest corner. It also never rises in the far southeast corner and sets in the far southwest corner.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב משרשיא said: These rules are not valid. For it was taught in a ברייתא: The sun has never risen from the northeast corner and set in the northwest corner. And the sun has never risen from the southeast corner and set in the southwest corner.
steps.whatsHappening: רב משרשיא rejects רבי יוסי's rules about the longest and shortest days. He proves his point from a ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוסי treated the summer path as marking true north and the winter path as marking true south. The ברייתא says the sun never reaches the real northern or southern corners, so those paths cannot mark exact north or south. What is left is the equinox, when the sun rises due east and sets due west.
steps.whyThisMatters: In practice, the only safe way to find the directions by the sun is at the equinoxes of ניסן and תשרי. The summer and winter paths cannot be used.

phrases.english: Rav Mesharshiya said:
These rules are not valid,
as it was taught: The sun has never risen
from the northeast corner
and set in the northwest corner,
and the sun has not risen
from the southeast corner
and set in the southwest corner.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב מְשַׁרְשְׁיָא: לֵיתַנְהוּ לְהָנֵי כְּלָלֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the summer and winter parts of רבי יוסי's method from step 13.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects using the longest-day and shortest-day sun paths to mark true north and south. The equinox method still stands.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The sun never rises or sets at the real northern or southern corners, so its solstice paths do not line up with the true directions.
steps.whatToRemember: רבי יוסי's backup method is mostly rejected. Only the equinox, when the sun rises due east and sets due west, can be trusted for finding directions by the sun.

steps.title: שמואל: The spring equinox begins at one of four quarter-points of the day
steps.stepSummary: Since the topic is the תקופות, שמואל teaches that תקופת ניסן always begins at one of four exact times: the start of the day, the start of the night, midday, or midnight.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמואל said: The spring equinox (תקופת ניסן) only falls at one of the four quarter-points of the day: either at the start of the day, or at the start of the night, or at midday, or at midnight.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a related topic about the תקופות. It brings שמואל's rule for exactly when the spring equinox begins.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the discussion turned to the equinoxes, שמואל adds a calendar rule. The equinox never starts at a random hour. It always lands on one of four fixed points, each one quarter of a full day apart. This works because, by שמואל's count, each year is a set number of days plus a quarter-day, so the starting time moves forward in steps of six hours.

keyTerms.meaning: The spring equinox, the start of the spring season
The four quarter-points of a full day (day and night together)

phrases.english: Shmuel said:
The spring equinox does not fall
except at the four quarters of the day,
either at the beginning of the day
or at the beginning of the night,
or at midday
or at midnight.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל: אֵין תְּקוּפַת נִיסָן נוֹפֶלֶת אֶלָּא בְּאַרְבָּעָה רִבְעֵי הַיּוֹם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Picks up the topic of the תקופות from steps 13-15 and starts a new discussion about when they occur.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: תקופת ניסן always begins at one of four fixed times: the start of the day, the start of the night, midday, or midnight.

steps.title: The fixed times for the summer, autumn, and winter seasons
steps.stepSummary: שמואל continues his chart. תקופת תמוז begins at 1.5 or 7.5 hours, תקופת תשרי at 3 or 9 hours, and תקופת טבת at 4.5 or 10.5 hours, counted into either the day or the night.
steps.simpleTranslation: The summer season (תמוז) begins only after 1.5 or 7.5 hours of the day or night. The autumn season (תשרי) begins only after 3 or 9 hours of the day or night. The winter season (טבת) begins only after 4.5 or 10.5 hours of the day or night.
steps.whatsHappening: שמואל finishes the list he started in Step 16. He now gives the possible start times for the other three seasons.
steps.deeperAnalysis: תקופת ניסן always begins at hour 0 or hour 6 of a day or night. Each later season adds 7.5 hours, so the start time moves forward by the same amount each time. That gives 1.5 or 7.5 for תמוז, 3 or 9 for תשרי, and 4.5 or 10.5 for טבת.

keyTerms.meaning: The summer season, beginning at the summer solstice
The autumn season, beginning at the autumn equinox
The winter season, beginning at the winter solstice
Whether in the day or in the night (the hours are counted from the start of either one)

steps.confusionAlert: The hours here are not clock times like 1:30. They count from the start of the day (about 6 AM) or the start of the night (about 6 PM). '1.5' means 1.5 hours after either of those points.

phrases.english: And the season of Tammuz does not fall except
either at one and a half hours,
or at seven and a half hours,
whether in the day or in the night.
And the season of Tishrei does not fall except

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ בְּשָׁלֹשׁ שָׁעוֹת אוֹ בְּתֵשַׁע שָׁעוֹת,
phrases.english: either at three hours or at nine hours,
whether in the day or in the night.
And the season of Teves does not fall except

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ בְּאַרְבַּע וּמֶחֱצָה אוֹ בְּעֶשֶׂר וּמֶחֱצָה,
phrases.english: either at four and a half or at ten and a half hours,
whether in the day or in the night.

steps.alternativePossibleLabel: Continuation of the מימרא in Step 16
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues שמואל's list from תקופת ניסן to the other three seasons
steps.mimraCoreRuling: תמוז begins at 1.5 or 7.5 hours, תשרי at 3 or 9 hours, and טבת at 4.5 or 10.5 hours, counted into either the day or the night.

steps.title: The math behind the chart: 91 days and 7.5 hours per season
steps.stepSummary: Each season lasts exactly 91 days and 7.5 hours. Because of this, each season begins half an hour later than the previous one in the rotation of planetary hours.
steps.simpleTranslation: Between one season and the next there are only 91 days and 7.5 hours. And each season is pushed later than the one before it by only half an hour.
steps.whatsHappening: שמואל continues his statement with the rule that explains all the times in the chart. It shows where the 7.5-hour jumps come from.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Four seasons of 91 days and 7.5 hours add up to 365¼ days, which is a full solar year. 91 days is exactly 13 weeks, so only the extra 7.5 hours shift things. The seven planetary hours repeat in a fixed cycle, and 7.5 hours is one full cycle plus half an hour. So each season begins half an hour later in that cycle.

keyTerms.meaning: Is drawn out or pushed later
Than its fellow, meaning the previous season

steps.whatToRemember: Year = 365¼ days. Each season = 91 days + 7.5 hours. Each season starts 7.5 hours later in the day than the one before, which is half an hour later in the planetary-hour cycle.

phrases.english: And there is not between one season and the next
except ninety-one days
and seven and a half hours.
And a season is not drawn later than its fellow
except by half an hour.

steps.alternativePossibleLabel: Explanatory part of the same מימרא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the underlying calculation that produces the start times listed in Steps 16 and 17
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Seasons are 91 days and 7.5 hours apart, and each starts half an hour later than the last in the planetary-hour cycle.

steps.title: Seasons that begin in the hour of Jupiter bring damage
steps.stepSummary: שמואל teaches that when תקופת ניסן falls in the hour of צדק, it breaks trees. When תקופת טבת falls in the hour of צדק, it dries up seeds. This is only true when the new moon appeared in the hour of לבנה or צדק.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמואל also said: whenever the spring season begins in the hour of Jupiter, it breaks the trees. Whenever the winter season begins in the hour of Jupiter, it dries up the seeds. But this is only when the new moon was born in the hour of the Moon or in the hour of Jupiter.
steps.whatsHappening: שמואל adds a new teaching about the seasons. He says what happens when a season begins during a particular planetary hour.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each hour is assigned to one of seven heavenly bodies in a fixed rotation. A season beginning in the hour of צדק (Jupiter) brings harm: strong winds that break trees in ניסן, or dryness that ruins seeds in טבת. The last line limits this rule. It only applies if the new moon also appeared in the hour of לבנה or צדק.

keyTerms.meaning: Jupiter, one of the seven heavenly bodies that rule the hours in rotation
That it was born, meaning the new moon appeared

steps.confusionAlert: Here צדק does not mean 'righteousness.' It is the name of the planet Jupiter, which rules certain hours.

phrases.english: And Shmuel said:

phrases.aramaic: אֵין לְךָ תְּקוּפַת נִיסָן שֶׁנּוֹפֶלֶת בְּצֶדֶק,
phrases.english: There is no spring season that falls in the hour of Jupiter
that does not break the trees.

phrases.aramaic: וְאֵין לְךָ תְּקוּפַת טֵבֵת שֶׁנּוֹפֶלֶת בְּצֶדֶק,
phrases.english: And there is no winter season that falls in the hour of Jupiter
that does not dry up the seeds.
And this is only when the new moon was born
either in the hour of the Moon or in the hour of Jupiter.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל: אֵין לְךָ תְּקוּפַת נִיסָן שֶׁנּוֹפֶלֶת בְּצֶדֶק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the planetary-hour rotation from Step 18 to describe the effects of specific season start times
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A ניסן or טבת season beginning in the hour of צדק damages trees or seeds, but only if the new moon appeared in the hour of לבנה or צדק.
